# Abstract

Legislators and their staff have limited time to serve constituents and advance policy goals. What determines their distribution of attention among constituents, potential donors, and policy goals? While scholarship has explored representational topics such as bill sponsorship, floor speeches, press releases, committee activity, and the like, much less is known about other, less visible forms of representation. In this paper, we contrast those traditional forms of representation against a much less visible form: how member’s advocate on behalf of their constituents, donors, and policy goals to federal agencies. By analyzing thousands of letters sent to government agencies by members of Congress, we develop new measures of legislator issue attention, specialization, and representational activity over time. 

We use these data to examine relationships between committee membership, seniority, electoral security, and the type of advocacy behavior in which members engage.  Existing theories focusing on institutional position suggest that committee membership and seniority should drive letter-writing behavior and that it will focus on oversight of the agency's policy work. In contrast, theories focusing on electoral incentives and the creation of the personal vote suggest that constituent and donor service should drive letter-writing behavior and that it will focus on securing agency resources for constituents. Scholars have found that both institutional position and electoral incentive shape corporate donor service. Our data allow new tests of these theories, not just on the public forms of representation traditionally studied, but on the more subterranean forms of representation that have substantive policy consequences and may only be monitored by political insiders, if at all.  

Do legislators shift attention to policy work as they gain seniority or electoral security? Do members in key fundraising positions or vulnerable districts disproportionately advocate on behalf of potential corporate supporters? Does a legislator's party or ideology influence the constituents on whose behalf legislators advocate? We address these questions with respect to which agencies legislators choose to contact, on whose behalf, and the distribution of attention to policy issues within and across federal agencies over time.

```{r means_by_type_table}
data <- df %>% 
  group_by(member_state, year, chamber) %>% 
  summarise(perYear = n()) %>% ungroup() %>%
  group_by(chamber) %>% 
  summarise(perType = round(mean(perYear))) %>% ungroup() %>%
```

```{r means_by_type, fig.height=2}
  # simple average
df %>% 
  filter(Type != "To be coded") %>%
  group_by(chamber, Type, name_state, year) %>% mutate(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>%
  group_by(chamber, Type) %>% summarise(perType = mean(n)) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(chamber) %>% mutate(mean = mean(perType), sd = sd(perType) ) %>% 
  mutate(sd.above.mean = (perType - mean)/sd ) %>% ungroup() %>%

  full_join(data) %>% 
  select(-mean, -sd) %>% 
ggplot() + 
  geom_tile(aes(x = Type, y = chamber, fill = sd.above.mean))  + 
  geom_text(aes(x = Type, y = chamber, label = round(perType, 0 ))) + 
  labs(title = paste("Average Correspondence per Year by Type"),
       x = "",
       y = "",
       fill = "SD Above Chamber Mean") + 
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```


#### Censoring 

Unfortunately, much our data are censored around the 2008-2009 and 2016-2017 party transitions, some the most informative time periods in our study period. 

Most right-censored series will be completed, but some agencies have changed systems such that logs are less useful or even terminated. For example, the DOL Office of Administrative Law Judges "discontinued the use of the spreadsheet" tracking congressional inquiries in November 2016. Similarly, DHS Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) may have stopped keeping its own log in 2014, even though this correspondence logged by ICE was distinct from correspondence addressed to ICE and logged by the DHS Secretary's Office.

Left censoring comes from two sources:
(1) Formal document retention cycles (agencies good at destroying documents such as the DOD and the FCC), and
(2) Document loss and changing systems (agencies bad at keeping documents). 
Either one of these may correlate with changes in an agency's salience due to changes in party control. It does seem that the most contacted/controversial agencies (EPA, DHS) keep very good records. This might lead us to a slight bias toward older records being about policy, but we do not see evidence of such bias in our data. Nevertheless, our timeseries analysis either subsets to agencies where we have full data or includes agency and/or Congress fixed effects.

#### Timing

Dates are generally the addressed date of the letter, but may alternatively be the date the letter was received by that agency---almost always within a few days. 

There might be some interesting signal in the formality of letterhead that changes things even when the agency knows what is coming. For example, the USGS recorded this note on a letter from McCain: "See all attachments including email string - Dave Applegate and John Godt are aware this is coming."


## Data Collection and Coding Process

This paper presents a new data set of letters, phone calls, and emails received by all federal agencies and subagencies. 

We developed a [codebook](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fJxjXjAyRL9vX-16fSsH29anXZc-W74GMf_7BSgWkws/edit) to classify correspondence by type and to identify referents such as agency rules, hearings, or legislation. Our coding process began with the authors coding a representative sample of records. We then trained undergraduate and graduate RAs. The first several thousand log entries were double coded. For example, of over 10,000 log entries for the Environmental Protection Agency, the first 2,500 were double-coded with inter-coder agreement of .9 where coders did not flag their coding as uncertain and  .78 overall. Throughout the hand-coding process, we also developed subagency-specific coding rules where agency staff consistently described certain types of correspondence with certain words. For example, where "rulemaking" consistently indicated that a legislator's request involved an agency rule, all cases yet uncoded by hand are assigned to be type "Policy-Rulemaking" for the present analysis. 



## To do:

### Near term

Get district demand characteristics from census

- industry codes (e.g.. Ag state percent farm)
- size of state = staffers in senate 
- the - bleed over - are you using staff to do policy work as well 
- normal vote in district - previous presidential return 

Get approps subcommittee membership data through the 115th

Crosswalk agencies and oversight committees

Correct committee data (there are some errors and missingness in appointment and termination dates)

### Longer term

Use coding rules, SVMs, or topic models to auto-code entries where human coders have given us a good deal of data (e.g. USDA with coding rules, EPA with a topic model or SVM), or develop coding rules based on unsupervised clustering where we have a lot of text (e.g. FERC, CDC). 

For many agencies, we have a sample of letters. These can be pasted into their respective Google sheets. This could be a productive way to skim a broad sample of letters and will provide more text for analysis. 

Use agencies where we have data on (some) calls and emails to estimate the bias in the letterhead correspondence that constitutes most logs. For example, DOD Defense Logistics received 8 calls but only 2 letters from members regarding the termination of a contract for parachutes, suggesting that letters may be a small portion of contacts for certain issues like corporate service. Between May 2015 and December 2017, the DOJ Office of Administrative Law Judges received 132 emails, 109 telephone calls, and only 54 letters. Between 2007 and 2017, the Postal Regulatory Commission received 100 emails, 30 faxes, 173 letters, 118 calls. 

Most agencies redact constituent names, but some have not, which may allow us to do some limited demographic analysis.

For USDA and a few others, we have logs of non-congressional letters; it may be interesting to compare Congressional attention to direct public/constituent attention. 


# Advocacy: A personal choice, enhanced by institutional power

## A few members advocate across agencies and topics

```{r gini}
library(ineq)
gini <- df %>% group_by(agency) %>% mutate(perAgency = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  filter(perAgency >100) %>% 
  group_by(member_state, agency, chamber, year) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(member_state, agency, chamber) %>% mutate(n = mean(n)) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(agency, chamber) %>% 
  mutate(byAgency = round(Gini(n),2)) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(chamber) %>%
  mutate(byChamber = round(Gini(n),2)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(chamber, agency, byChamber, byAgency) %>% distinct() %>% arrange(byAgency)
```

  The volume of correspondence per legislator is highly unequal. Within the `r length(unique(gini$agency))` agencies receiving more than 100 letters, the Gini coefficient of letters per member per year is `r unique(gini$byChamber[which(gini$chamber=="Senate")])` for Senators and `r unique(gini$byChamber[which(gini$chamber=="House")])` for Representatives, similar to income inequality estimates for Mexico and the United States respectively and higher than inequality in campaign spending (The Gini coefficient for House campaign spending in 2016 was .29).  
  
  
  
```{r quartiles}
quartiles <- df %>% 
  group_by(member_state, chamber, year) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
  group_by(member_state, chamber) %>% mutate(mean = mean(n)) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(chamber) %>% mutate(quartile = ntile(mean, 4)) %>% 
  group_by(quartile, chamber) %>% summarise(n = sum(n)) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(top = ifelse(quartile ==4, T, F)) %>% 
  group_by(top, chamber) %>% 
  summarise(tvb = sum(n)) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(chamber) %>% mutate(percent = round(100*tvb/sum(tvb), 0)) %>% 
  filter(top == T)
```
In terms of letters per year, the top 25% of Senators and Representatives write `r quartiles$percent[2]` and `r quartiles$percent[1]` percent of all letters from each chamber. 

This skewed distribution holds across types of advocacy. As illustrated below, whether it is policy advocacy, lobbying on behalf of corporations, or individual-level constituent service a small number of legislators are doing a disproportionate share of letters. Moreover, it is often the same legislators engaging in constituent service and policy advocacy. When ranked by overall volume of correspondence, regardless of type, the top quartile of members are disproportionately amount of advocacy for individuals, nonprofits, local governments, and policy. Advocacy on behalf of business interests is notably more diffuse.

## What distinguishes letter-writers? 

###  Constituent demand for advocacy

The number of constituents asking for assistance is a major driver of member advocacy. 

```{r sentate_percapita_map, fig.height=4}
Chamber = "Senate"

df %>% 
  filter(chamber == Chamber) %>% 
  group_by(state, Type) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>%
# map_id creates the aesthetic mapping to the state name column
ggplot() + 
  # map points to the fifty_states shape data
  geom_map(aes(map_id = state, fill = n), map = fifty_states) + 
  expand_limits(x = fifty_states$long, y = fifty_states$lat) +
```

## Specialization

Theories rooted in institutional position suggest that committee members, especially committee chairs will focus on governmental activities where they have formal oversight authority and responsibilities and where constituent service this authority may advantage them in securing benefits for constituents and potential donors. 

Our data show limited support for the importance of formal oversight powers in directing the attention of committee members. In some case, like the Agriculture and Judiciary, we see strong relationships between the committee on which one sits and the agencies they lobby. In many other case, however, members of committees with formal oversight powers are not the most attentive. Instead, members of certain committees tend to lobby widely across the federal bureaucracy. 

In the Senate, these high-contact committees align with those considered 'prestige' committees along with Aging, Agriculture, Banking, Health, and Judiciary committees. Prestige Senate committees are consistently on the high end of distribution of requests coming in to each agency.

```{r committee_deptSenate}
Chamber <- "Senate"
# zeros
zeros <- data_frame(
  committee = rep(unique(dcommittees$committee[dcommittees$chamber == Chamber]), n_distinct(dcommittees$department) ), 
  department =  rep(unique(dcommittees$department), n_distinct(dcommittees$committee[dcommittees$chamber == Chamber]) ),
  n = 0) %>%
  mutate(committee_dept = paste(committee, department)) %>% 
  filter(!committee_dept %in% dcommittees$committee_dept,  !is.na(department))

data <- dcommittees %>% 
  filter(chamber == Chamber) %>% 
  filter(!department %in% c("PRC", "NASA", "FCA", "Amtrak", "RRB")) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(committee), !committee %in% c("PRINTING", "MINORITY WHIP", "MINORITY LEADER", "MAJORITY WHIP", "MAJORITY LEADER", "LIBRARY", "ETHICS", "SPEAKER", "INVESTIGATE THE VOTING IRREGULARITIES OF AUGUST 2", "HOUSE ADMINISTRATION", "EVENTS SURROUNDING THE 2012 TERRORIST ATTACK ON BENGHAZI", "ASSISTANT MINORITY LEADER"))%>% 
  group_by(committee, department, chamber, year) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(committee, department, chamber) %>% summarise(n = mean(n)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  full_join(zeros) %>% 
  filter(!department %in% c("PRC", "NASA", "FCA", "Amtrak", "RRB")) %>% 
  filter( !is.na(department), !is.na(committee), !committee %in% c("PRINTING", "MINORITY WHIP", "MINORITY LEADER", "MAJORITY WHIP", "MAJORITY LEADER", "LIBRARY", "ETHICS", "SPEAKER", "INVESTIGATE THE VOTING IRREGULARITIES OF AUGUST 2", "HOUSE ADMINISTRATION", "EVENTS SURROUNDING THE 2012 TERRORIST ATTACK ON BENGHAZI", "ASSISTANT MINORITY LEADER", "ENERGY INDEPENDENCE", "DEFICIT REDUCTION", "STANDARDS OF OFFICIAL CONDUCT"))%>% 
  group_by(department) %>% mutate(mean = mean(n), sd = sd(n)) %>% 
  mutate(above = n - mean) %>% 
  mutate(sd.above.mean = above/sd) %>% ungroup %>%
  mutate(prestige = ifelse(committee %in% c( "RULES", "BUDGET", "WAYS", "COMMERCE", 
                                             "APPROPRIATIONS", "ARMED SERVICES", "FINANCE", "FOREIGN RELATIONS"), "Prestige", "Not prestige") ) 
  
  ggplot(data) + # plot
  geom_tile(aes(x = department, y = committee, fill = sd.above.mean))  + 
  geom_text(aes(x = department, y = committee, label = round(n, 0 ))) +
  facet_grid(prestige ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(title = paste(Chamber, "Committee Correspondence per Year per Department or Agency 2007-2017"),
       x = "Department",
       y = "") + 
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = .8))

```

In the House, the Transportation, Energy, Financial Services, Armed Services, and Appropriations Committees are the most active. Notably, members of the Budget, Rules, and Ways and Means committees, often considered prestige appointments, are not as active.

## Institutional position: formal and informal power

### Committee appointment

Committee membership brings access to information, voting responsibilities, and prestige. Additionally, committee chairs have agenda control and additional staff. Some hypothesize that taking on leadership positions diverts attention from constituency service toward policy oversight. In contrast, others hypothesize that members will leverage the resources of office to better serve their constituents. How does a member's behavior change when they are appointed chair of a powerful committee? Does committee appointment lead to more policy work or constituent service?


*To do: *Committee member effect, chair effect

```{r chair_effect}
tenure <- dcommittees %>%
  filter(chair_since_2007 == T, Type2 == "Policy") %>% 
  mutate(tenure = as.numeric(year) - firstassignedchair) %>%
  group_by(bioname, tenure, department) %>% 
  summarise(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  filter(!is.na(tenure)) %>% 
  mutate(n = round(n, 1))

year.before.chair.DOL <- round(mean(tenure$n[tenure$tenure == -1 & tenure$department == "DOL"]), 1)
year.after.chair.DOL <- round(mean(tenure$n[tenure$tenure == 0 & tenure$department == "DOL"]), 1)

tenure %<>%
  group_by(bioname, tenure) %>% 
  summarise(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  filter(!is.na(tenure)) %>% 
  mutate(n = round(n, 1))

year.before.chair <- round(mean(tenure$n[tenure$tenure == -1]), 1)
year.after.chair <- round(mean(tenure$n[tenure$tenure == 0]), 1)

#Ritchie (2017) finds the mean number of policy-relevant letters to the Department of Labor is higher for members of their oversight committee 10.4, compared to non-members (7.7).

```

Averaging across all departments and committees, we find a increase from `r year.before.chair` to `r year.after.chair` policy-relevant letters. However, there is significant variation among committee chairs and it is not clear that formal oversight authority accounts for this increase. 

Committee chair appointment is most impactful in the House with respect to policy advocacy.

Committee chair appointments seem to be especially important in the house and most members appear to write slightly more letters after being appointed to chair. However, the density of correspondence by member misses the most interesting dynamic: The volume of correspondence is highly unequal, even across committee chairs. Indeed just three chairs initiated the majority of correspondence.


When we match committees and departments, we see some larger effects, but not consistently. For example, Science and Environment committee chairs averaged more letters to EPA after becoming chair, but they also wrote more to DOT. Similarly, Transportation chairs wrote more to both DOT and EPA, so, while becoming chair generally matters, changes in correspondence behavior are broader than changes in formal oversight powers. 

Focusing on committee effects, chair-committee linkages seem stronger in the House than the Senate where non-chair members are also engaged. Committee leadership appears to mean more in the House, where most members do very little. This is especially clear for DHS where House Homeland Security Committee leaders write far more to DHS than other members but a half dozen Senators write more letters to DHS than the Homeland Security Committee Chair.

```{r committeechiars_barcode_DHS, fig.height=3}
Chamber = "House" 
dcommittees %>% 
  filter(chamber == Chamber, 
         committee == "HOMELAND SECURITY",
         chair_since_2007 == T,  
         complete == T, 
         agency != "PRC", 
         DATE < as.Date("2017-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = DATE, 
        y = chair, 
        color = department),
    shape = 73
  ) +
  geom_segment(aes(y = chair, yend = chair, 
                   x = assigneddate, xend = terminationdate, 
                   linetype = factor(position)),
               position = position_nudge(y = -0.3)) +
  labs(title = paste(Chamber, "Committee Chairs"),
       y = "", 
       x = "" ) +
  scale_y_discrete(position = "right") +
  theme(
    strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 180),
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) + 
  facet_grid(committee ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "both") 
```

Some members, even committee chairs, and especially senators, distribute their attention across a wide variety of agencies. These distributions are fairly consistent over time. 

*to do:* committee members over time. 

Two results are particularly interesting: (1) we find surprisingly weak committee-agency associations (this holds when we subset to policy letters) and (2) chairs and ranking minority members are often not the top letter-writers to the agencies they oversee (e.g. Ag Committee chairs are not top letter-writers to USDA, though Senate Environment Committee and House Energy, Oversight, and Science Committees are top letter-writers to EPA). Despite the advantages that chairs have in additional staff and formal authority (some agencies even have written policies about prioritizing correspondence from the chair their oversight committee), other members often exceed them in their volume of correspondence.

**TO DO:**  committee chairs over time. 

Comparing within-members over time, committee chair appointments occasionally reshape behavior a great deal (e.g. House Oversight) but most committee chair's distribution of attention is more a function of their previous behavior than their position. This is stark in the House Homeland Security Committee where Chair King seems to attend to the same distribution of agencies before and after being appointed chair, while Chair McCaul seems more affected by taking on the chair position. 


### Advocates and non-advocates

Some members write significantly more letters per year than others, and those who write do so across issues and agencies. For example, Senator Schumer lobbies more than anyone on behalf of local governments and nonprofits, but he is also among those Senators lobbying most on behalf of individuals and companies and on policy issues. As chair of the Rules committee, Senator Shumer has little official oversight authority but nevertheless, increased both policy and constituent service advocacy upon becoming chair. Arlen Specter is another top advocate. Indeed, a full year after being defeated in the Primary and months after leaving office, Specter was still writing letters to federal agencies.

### Does advocacy behavior vary over time?

We find that most members are not hyper-focused in their letter-writing behavior, even regarding policy issues. However, many members do have distinctive patterns of activity that seem to remain fairly consistent over time, even across changes in committee membership. The plots below represent these patterns as a "bar-code" for each member with each line marking a letter.

```{r members_barcoded, fig.height=16, fig.width=11}
# barcode plot of committee members 


Chamber <- "Senate" # "House" #  
 
# member by year by agency 
df %>% 
  filter(chamber == Chamber, complete == T) %>% 
  group_by(name_state) %>% mutate(n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>% 
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = DATE, 
        y = reorder(name_state, n), # sort by total number of lewters writen
        color = department), 
    # alpha = .6,
    shape = 73,
    size=2
  ) +
  labs(title = paste(Chamber),
       y = paste("Members by", "Total Number of Letters"), 
       x = "Date of Correspondence" ) +
  theme(
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size=5)
  ) + 
    guides(fill=guide_legend(ncol=1)) 

```
Subsetting to members appointed to serve as a committee chair, we see that subsequent chairs of the same committee often target a very different set of agencies, suggesting that there is a lot to be said for style over institutional position or events of the day
